claims.proposition_evaluated: The City of Edmonton's automated counters recorded at least 1.10 million and fewer than 1.50 million bicycle passages from 2026-01-01 through 2026-07-31 inclusive.
claims.interpretation_notes: The City labels the observations cyclist counts. I treated 'trips' in the circulating wording as counter passages, not distinct people or journeys. A secondary analysis reported approximately 1.29 million and would produce Supported under both cutoff sets, but I could not verify that the specified base dataset covered the full period through July 31.

supporting_evidence.finding: A CBC analysis of Edmonton's published daily counter data reported nearly 1.3 million cyclist counts from January 1 through July 31, 2026.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Are people actually using Edmonton's bike lanes? Here's a look at the numbers
supporting_evidence.source_publisher: CBC News, republished by Yahoo News
supporting_evidence.establishes: An independent secondary analysis reported a total within both of the brief's Supported bands.

challenging_evidence.finding: The API metadata available during review listed the base dataset's last update as 2026-07-22, before the required period ended. The dataset also warns that full days may be incomplete and that the raw data have not undergone quality control or quality assurance.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Bike and Pedestrian Counts (Eco Counter), dataset tq23-qn4m
challenging_evidence.source_date: Last updated 2026-07-22 according to the consulted metadata
challenging_evidence.establishes: The consulted primary-source metadata did not verify complete base-dataset coverage through July 31, which the frozen verdict rule requires.

limitations: The required base dataset is Bike and Pedestrian Counts (Eco Counter), tq23-qn4m. The separate counter-location dataset is Bike Counter Locations (Eco Counter), py7x-4d39.
The published observations are raw cyclist counts or passages. They are not distinct riders or journeys: one rider can generate multiple counts, and a ride can pass multiple counters.
I could not reproduce the full-window aggregation, number of reporting counters, missing-day count, location-type split, or busiest-counter share from the primary dataset interface.
The secondary 1.29 million result cannot cure an unverified end date under the brief's explicit short-window rule.
No verified same-window totals for 2024 and 2025 were obtained.
The primary and alternative threshold classifications would both be Supported if a complete primary extract confirmed 1.29 million passages through July 31.
unknowns: The last timestamp actually present in tq23-qn4m as of 2026-09-03.
The exact January-through-July total in the specified base dataset.
How many counters contributed and how many counter-days were missing.
Whether counters were added, moved, removed, or affected by known configuration errors during the period.

missing_evidence.description: A complete, timestamped export of tq23-qn4m through 2026-07-31, together with the aggregation query and missing-day audit.
Equivalent audited extracts for January through July 2024 and 2025.

calculations_needed: Sum total_cyclist_count for 2026-01-01 through 2026-07-31 inclusive after excluding pedestrian-only records, and enumerate distinct reporting counters and missing counter-days.
Repeat the identical calculation for 2024 and 2025.

A complete total from 1.10 million to below 1.50 million would change the primary verdict to Supported; 0.65 million to below 1.10 million or 1.50 million to 1.95 million would change it to Partially supported; outside those limits would change it to Contradicted.
claims.suggested_one_line: A secondary analysis reported about 1.29 million cyclist counts, but complete July coverage in the specified base dataset was not independently verified, so the strict full-window claim is not established.
claims.suggested_short_answer: The reported total is plausible and falls within both Supported bands, but the primary record consulted did not verify coverage through July 31.
suggested_tldr: Counters measure passages, not distinct people or journeys.
CBC reported about 1.29 million through July 31.
The consulted base-dataset metadata showed a July 22 last update, leaving the required full window unverified.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Every counter in the brief's non-empty set of live, classifiable, sufficiently measured automated counters on Edmonton on-street bike lanes had a July 2025 median below 25 bicycle passages per day.
claims.interpretation_notes: The proposition covers only metered on-street lanes selected by the brief's five tests, not all Edmonton bike lanes and not the accuracy of residents' momentary observations. The alternative cutoff is 50 passages per day. I could not reproducibly construct the required verdict set, so neither cutoff can be applied.

challenging_evidence.finding: The City's implementation guide reports approximately 205,000 bicycle crossings during 2021 at 83 Avenue west of 99 Street. Dividing by 365 gives approximately 562 passages per day, although this is an annual mean from an earlier year rather than the required July 2025 median.
challenging_evidence.establishes: At least one historically monitored Edmonton bicycle corridor carried traffic far above either low-use cutoff, challenging a blanket characterization while not determining the frozen verdict set.

challenging_evidence.finding: The same guide reports 2,796 daily downtown bicycle counts in June 2017 and 6,501 in June 2018 across multiple count locations.
challenging_evidence.establishes: Older multi-location measurements are inconsistent with describing all monitored cycling infrastructure as unused, but they are not per-counter July 2025 medians.

limitations: The required sources are counts dataset tq23-qn4m, locations dataset py7x-4d39, and Bike Routes dataset vd4b-a4iv.
I could not execute the nearest-segment spatial join or enumerate the complete results of tests 1 through 5 from the public interfaces available during review.
The consulted counts sample identified Hermitage South as pedestrian-only, so that record cannot establish bicycle volume for the named Hermitage corridor.
I did not obtain verified counter matches for 119 Avenue, 132 Avenue between 97 and 127 Street, or the Whyte Avenue area.
The counters are selected monitoring locations, not a representative sample of all Edmonton lanes. Unmetered lanes remain outside the proposition.
A missing or failed counter is not evidence that a lane carried no traffic.
The counts dataset is raw, may omit complete portions of days, and has not undergone published QA/QC.
Because the verdict set, unclassifiable counters, and under-reported counters were not established, both the 25-per-day and 50-per-day verdicts are Not established.
unknowns: The complete cyclist-counter universe and which counters had records on 2025-07-01.
Which counters join within 30 metres to built ON ROAD routes, which are OFF ROAD, and which are unclassifiable or borderline.
Which otherwise eligible counters went out of service by 2025-07-31.
Whether every remaining counter recorded at least 20 July days.
The July median, busiest July day, January median, and 2025 total for every member of the verdict set.
The share of Edmonton's on-street bike-lane kilometres represented by the counters.
Whether manual counts exist for each named corridor.

missing_evidence.description: A reproducible counter-by-counter output of all five membership tests, including spatial distances, classifications, service dates, and July completeness.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton Open Data or a reviewer able to export and spatially join the three datasets

missing_evidence.description: Per-counter July and January daily aggregates and 2025 annual totals for the resulting verdict set.
Published manual or short-duration bicycle and motor-vehicle counts for the four named corridors.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton Transportation Planning and Operations

calculations_needed: Apply tests 1 through 5 exactly as frozen, list every inclusion and exclusion, and stop with Not established if the set is empty, any candidate is unclassifiable, or any included counter is under-reported.
For every included counter, calculate the median of daily bicycle counts in July 2025, maximum July day, January median, and 2025 sum.
Classify once at below 25 per day and again at below 50 per day.

If every included counter were below 25, the primary verdict would become Supported; if some but not all were below 25, Partially supported; if none were below 25, Contradicted.
claims.suggested_one_line: The required counter set and July medians could not be reproducibly established, while older City measurements show that at least some monitored corridors have carried hundreds of bicycle passages per day.
claims.suggested_short_answer: The public record consulted was insufficient to apply the brief's five-test rule, so the metered-lane claim is not established.
suggested_tldr: The verdict requires a complete spatial and service-status audit.

claims.proposition_evaluated: No more than about 2 percent of City of Edmonton residents rode a bicycle at least once during the preceding twelve months, as measured by a representative Edmonton population survey.
claims.interpretation_notes: The claim concerns annual participation among residents, not bicycle trips, commuters, bicycle ownership, counter passages, or distinct bike-lane users. No admissible estimate was found, so neither the primary nor alternative thresholds can be applied.

challenging_evidence.finding: A 2014 City of Edmonton Insight Community survey received 646 responses from 1,029 invited panel members: 306 respondents reported warm-weather cycling and 66 reported year-round cycling. Reviewer arithmetic gives 372/646, or 57.6 percent, riding in at least one season.
challenging_evidence.source_title: How does the inclination to bicycle sway the decision to ride in warm and winter seasons?
challenging_evidence.establishes: The located Edmonton panel result is far above both ceilings, but the opt-in, non-random panel is not admissible as a population estimate.

challenging_evidence.finding: The Canadian Community Health Survey asks whether respondents bicycled in the previous twelve months, but its public-use geography is health region rather than the City of Edmonton or Edmonton CMA.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Canadian Community Health Survey questionnaire and public-use microdata documentation
challenging_evidence.establishes: A suitable twelve-month question exists nationally, but no released result at the brief's required geography was identified.

limitations: The search covered City bike-ridership surveys, the Canadian Community Health Survey, the 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey, the Navigating Tomorrow successor, and Alberta or Edmonton survey leads as of 2026-09-03.
The 2014 Insight Community was a non-random opt-in online panel and cannot carry a population verdict.
The CCHS public-use file publishes health-region geography, not the City of Edmonton or Edmonton CMA.
The 2015 household travel survey is a one-weekday, 24-hour trip diary rather than a twelve-month participation instrument.
Navigating Tomorrow was operating continuously in 2025, but the City page consulted did not publish successor results by the as-of date.

The forms '.001% of the population' and '500 people using the bike lanes 4 months of the year' concern distinct lane users. No published instrument found measures that numerator, and no participation figure was set against them.
unknowns: The twelve-month cycling-participation rate for City of Edmonton residents.
Whether Statistics Canada, Alberta Health, or the City holds an unpublished custom tabulation at City geography.
Participation by children, since some candidate surveys cover only older age groups.
How many distinct residents use Edmonton bike lanes.

missing_evidence.description: A published probability or otherwise representative City of Edmonton survey asking whether residents rode a bicycle at least once in the preceding twelve months.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton, Statistics Canada, or Alberta Health

calculations_needed: If an admissible share P is published, apply the primary cutoffs: Supported at or below 2.5 percent, Partially supported above 2.5 through 5.0 percent, and Contradicted above 5.0 percent.
Apply the alternative cutoffs separately: Supported at or below 3.0 percent, Partially supported above 3.0 through 6.0 percent, and Contradicted above 6.0 percent.

what_would_change_my_verdict: A representative published Edmonton twelve-month participation estimate would replace Not established with the classification dictated by the fixed cutoffs.
claims.suggested_one_line: No representative published survey was found measuring whether Edmonton residents rode during the preceding year; the only located Edmonton seasonal result came from a non-random opt-in panel.
claims.suggested_short_answer: The one-to-two-percent population claim is not established because no admissible Edmonton annual participation estimate was identified.
suggested_tldr: Trips, commuting, ownership, and counter passages are not annual participation.
The located Insight result was an opt-in panel, not a representative sample.
Distinct bike-lane users remain unmeasured.

claims.proposition_evaluated: No more than 1 percent of City of Edmonton residents ride a bicycle year-round, and fewer than 15 percent ride during the non-winter portion of the same year, with both shares measured by one representative Edmonton sample.
claims.interpretation_notes: The circulating wording referred to people who use bike lanes. The normalized proposition openly substitutes the nearest potentially measurable quantity, residents who ride bicycles. It does not establish seasonal lane use. No admissible seasonal population split was found. The result is Not established under both the 2-percent and 3-percent Part A cutoffs.

challenging_evidence.finding: The 2014 Edmonton Insight Community panel classified 66 of 646 respondents, or 10.2 percent, as year-round cyclists and 306 of 646, or 47.4 percent, as warm-weather-only cyclists.
challenging_evidence.source_title: How does the inclination to bicycle sway the decision to ride in warm and winter seasons?
challenging_evidence.establishes: Both panel percentages exceed the asserted ceilings, but the non-random opt-in sample cannot establish Edmonton population prevalence.

challenging_evidence.finding: A City webpage says an estimated one in four cyclists rides all year and reports more than 90,000 counter-recorded movements in December 2023.
challenging_evidence.establishes: Winter riding occurs at material levels, but one in four cyclists uses cyclists rather than all residents as its denominator, and counter movements are passages rather than people.

limitations: No representative source was identified that published both seasonal shares for City of Edmonton residents from one sample.
The Insight Community categories were warm-weather-only cycling and year-round cycling including severe winter conditions, but the sample was non-random and opt-in.
Part B is only a ceiling: any admissible share below 15 percent would satisfy it.
The original wording concerned lane users. No public instrument found counts distinct people using bike lanes by season.
Counter volume cannot be substituted for population participation, so the December count was not used to decide either part.
This claim shares the participation-source search with one-to-two-percent-of-population-rides but requires the additional seasonal split.
unknowns: The year-round and non-winter participation shares among all Edmonton residents.
The share of annual counter passages occurring in a consistently defined winter period.
How many distinct residents use bike lanes in winter or other seasons.

missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton, Statistics Canada, or Alberta Health

missing_evidence.description: A complete annual counter extract and a predeclared winter-month definition for the contextual winter-volume share.

claims.suggested_short_answer: Neither the year-round nor non-winter population share is established, and no conclusion about distinct bike-lane users can be drawn.
suggested_tldr: The normalized claim measures riding, not lane use.
The located seasonal split was from a non-random panel.
Counter passages are context, not participation.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Bicycle was the main mode for approximately 2 percent of all weekday trips made by City of Edmonton residents in the most recent Edmonton household travel survey published by 2026-09-03.
claims.interpretation_notes: The most recent published result located was the 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey. It reports 54,800 bicycle trips among 3,139,100 weekday trips by City residents: 1.7 percent at the report's displayed precision and 2 percent in a rounded table. This is Supported under both threshold sets.

supporting_evidence.finding: The 2015 survey reports 54,800 bicycle trips out of 3,139,100 total weekday trips by City of Edmonton residents, publishing the bicycle mode share as 1.7 percent.
supporting_evidence.source_title: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report
supporting_evidence.establishes: The directly measured City weekday-trip share falls within the primary Supported range of 1.5 to 2.5 percent and the alternative range of 1.2 to 3.0 percent.

supporting_evidence.finding: The survey sampled approximately 15,300 City households and collected a 24-hour weekday travel diary during fall 2015, with weighting intended to represent the resident population.
supporting_evidence.source_title: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report
supporting_evidence.establishes: The figure comes from a large household travel survey and has the correct all-trips denominator.

challenging_evidence.finding: The Edmonton Region outside the City recorded 10,600 bicycle trips among 1,331,800 weekday trips, or 0.8 percent. This is below the primary range but is a different required geography and does not refute the City result.
challenging_evidence.source_title: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report
challenging_evidence.establishes: The result is geography-sensitive and must not be generalized to the wider region.

challenging_evidence.finding: The Statistics Canada table named in the discussion is a main-mode-of-commuting table, not a measure of all trips.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Main mode of commuting for the 10 largest census metropolitan areas, May 2021 to May 2025
challenging_evidence.establishes: The cited Statistics Canada table cannot independently support or refute an all-trips mode share.

The report does not establish that the bicycle share is higher specifically in neighbourhoods with bike infrastructure.
This claim and riders-are-recreational-not-commuters use the same 2015 survey: this claim takes bicycle trips over all trips, while the other takes purpose categories over bicycle trips.
unknowns: The current post-2015 bicycle share of all trips.
Weekend bicycle mode share.
Whether a published sub-area analysis isolates neighbourhoods with bike infrastructure.

missing_evidence.description: Published results from the Navigating Tomorrow successor survey, including City weekday and weekend mode shares.

The required regional alternative is 10,600 divided by 1,331,800 = approximately 0.8 percent.

The City result is Supported under both the primary and alternative cutoffs; the regional alternative would be Contradicted under the primary cutoffs and Partially supported under the alternative cutoffs.

claims.suggested_one_line: The latest published household survey found bicycle was the main mode for 1.7 percent of City residents' weekday trips in 2015, a fair 'about 2 percent' description.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Supported, but the figure comes from a fall 2015 weekday survey and should not be presented as current.
suggested_tldr: City result: 54,800 bicycle trips out of 3,139,100 weekday trips.
Published share: 1.7 percent.
The wider region's 0.8 percent is a different geography.

claims.proposition_evaluated: In the 2021 Census reference week, fewer than 1 percent of employed City of Edmonton residents with a usual workplace or no fixed workplace, excluding people working at home, reported bicycle as their main mode of commuting.
claims.interpretation_notes: Statistics Canada published 3,355 bicycle commuters among 380,315 people in the main-mode universe, or 0.9 percent. The result is Supported under both the below-1.0-percent primary cutoff and below-1.1-percent alternative cutoff.

supporting_evidence.finding: The 2021 Census Profile for the City of Edmonton reports 3,355 bicycle commuters among 380,315 commuters in the applicable main-mode universe, publishing a 0.9-percent bicycle share.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Census Profile, 2021 Census of Population: Edmonton, City (Census subdivision)
supporting_evidence.establishes: The published City share is below both frozen Supported cutoffs.

supporting_evidence.finding: For the Edmonton census metropolitan area, the same variable records 3,905 bicycle commuters among 537,645 commuters, or 0.7 percent.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Census Profile, 2021 Census of Population: Edmonton CMA

challenging_evidence.source_title: Census Profile, 2021 Census of Population: Edmonton, City
challenging_evidence.establishes: The 2021 reference week had an unusually large excluded work-at-home population, materially limiting comparisons with ordinary commuting conditions.

limitations: The census universe is employed persons aged 15 and over in private households with a usual place of work or no fixed workplace address, excluding those who worked at home.

claims.proposition_evaluated: More than half of bicycle trips made by City of Edmonton residents were recreational rather than work-related in the most recent household travel survey published by 2026-09-03.
claims.interpretation_notes: I mapped the report's 'HB Social/Rec' category to recreation and 'HB Work' plus 'NHB Work' to commuting or work. The other categories—HB PSE, HB School, HB Shopping, HB Personal Business, HB Pick up/Drop off, HB Other, and NHB Other—remain named third purposes. Because the report publishes rounded bicycle shares within each purpose rather than a direct purpose distribution of bicycle trips, the resulting estimates are approximate. They nevertheless put recreation below 35 percent and work above recreation, producing Contradicted under both cutoff sets.

supporting_evidence.finding: The survey reports 399,800 home-based social/recreation trips by all modes, of which a rounded 3 percent used bicycle. This implies approximately 11,994 recreational bicycle trips, or 21.9 percent of the published 54,800 bicycle-trip total.
supporting_evidence.source_title: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report
supporting_evidence.establishes: Recreation was a material bicycle-trip purpose, but the estimate is far below a majority.

challenging_evidence.finding: The report lists 650,700 home-based work trips with a rounded 3-percent bicycle share and 185,800 non-home-based work trips with a rounded 1-percent bicycle share. Reviewer arithmetic implies approximately 21,379 work-related bicycle trips, or 39.0 percent of the 54,800 bicycle-trip total, exceeding the estimated 21.9-percent recreation share.
challenging_evidence.source_title: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report
challenging_evidence.establishes: The published purpose-by-mode table points against both a recreational majority and a recreational plurality over work.

challenging_evidence.finding: The source reports an average City bicycle trip length of 4.1 kilometres; it does not publish a median bicycle-trip distance in the summary.
challenging_evidence.source_title: 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report
challenging_evidence.establishes: The distance evidence provides limited context for the 'usually within a short distance' wording but does not establish trip purpose.

limitations: The survey was conducted in fall 2015 on weekdays and published in April 2018; it is eleven years old at the as-of date.

The report gives purpose totals for all modes and rounded whole-percent bicycle shares within each purpose, not direct bicycle-purpose counts. All purpose-specific bicycle counts and shares here are reviewer calculations.
Multiplying every purpose total by its rounded bicycle percentage produces approximately 56,605 bicycle trips, rather than the published 54,800, demonstrating rounding error.
The 'HB Social/Rec' category may combine social visits and recreation; it is not necessarily limited to exercise or leisure rides.
The summary report does not publish the unweighted bicycle-trip sample size, limiting precision assessment.
No direct Edmonton bicycle-purpose distribution from the Navigating Tomorrow successor was found by 2026-09-03.
Counter time-of-day patterns cannot establish trip purpose and were not used for the verdict.
This claim and two-percent-of-trips-by-bike use the same 2015 survey: this claim estimates purpose shares within bicycle trips, whereas the other measures bicycle trips over all trips.
unknowns: The current bicycle trip-purpose distribution.
The exact unrounded bicycle counts in each purpose category.
The share of recreational rides that begin and end at the same place and whether the diary captured them consistently.
The median bicycle-trip distance.

missing_evidence.description: An unrounded City-level cross-tabulation of bicycle trips by the survey's purpose categories, including the weighted and unweighted bicycle-trip sample.
Published bicycle-purpose results from the Navigating Tomorrow successor survey.

calculations_needed: Recreation estimate: 399,800 HB Social/Rec trips multiplied by 3 percent = approximately 11,994; divided by 54,800 bicycle trips = approximately 21.9 percent.
Work estimate: (650,700 HB Work multiplied by 3 percent) plus (185,800 NHB Work multiplied by 1 percent) = approximately 21,379; divided by 54,800 = approximately 39.0 percent.
Because recreation is below 35 percent and work exceeds recreation, the primary result is Contradicted.
